choices.text: 3 — `copy` is a separate array
4 — both names point at the same array
3 — `const` prevents the array from being modified
It throws, because `list` is declared `const`

items.explanation: `const` binds the name, not the value. Assigning an array copies the reference, so both names see the same object. Copying the contents needs `[...list]` or `list.slice()`.

items.prompt:
Three independent API calls each take about 300 ms. The code awaits them one after another and the page takes ~900 ms to fill.

Which change makes it ~300 ms?

choices.text: Remove the `await` keywords so the calls do not block
Start all three, then `await Promise.all([...])` on the resulting promises
Move the calls into a `useEffect` so they run after render
Wrap each call in `setTimeout(..., 0)`

items.explanation: Sequential awaits mean each call starts only after the previous resolves. `Promise.all` needs the promises to already be in flight — which is why the calls are started first and awaited together. Dropping `await` starts them concurrently but leaves you with no values.

items.prompt: A click handler calls `setCount(count + 1)` three times in a row. `count` starts at 0. What is it after one click?

choices.text: 1, because all three reads see the same stale `count` from this render
0, because state updates are discarded inside an event handler
3, but only after a second render

items.explanation: `count` is a value captured by this render, not a live cell. All three calls compute 0 + 1. The updater form — `setCount(c => c + 1)` — is passed the latest value each time and gives 3.

items.prompt:
A list of editable rows is rendered with the array index as the `key`. A row is deleted from the middle, and afterwards the text a user had typed in one input shows up in a different row.

Why?

choices.text: The delete mutated the array instead of replacing it
Index keys are reused after the delete, so React matches the old element to a different item and keeps its DOM state
The inputs are uncontrolled and should be controlled
The parent did not re-render, so the DOM is stale

items.explanation: A key tells React which item an element belongs to across renders. With index keys, deleting the middle item shifts every later item onto a key that used to belong to its neighbour, so React reuses that DOM node — including whatever was typed into it. A stable id fixes it.

items.prompt:
A component fetches a user by `id` in a `useEffect` and sets state with the result. Rapidly switching between two users sometimes leaves the wrong user's data on screen.

What is the cause?

choices.text: The dependency array is missing `id`, so the effect never re-runs
Two requests are in flight and the slower one resolves last, overwriting the newer result
React batches the two state updates and keeps the first
The component is not memoised, so it renders twice

items.explanation: This is a race, not a dependency bug — the effect ran correctly both times. The fix is to make the stale response harmless: a cleanup function that flips an `ignore` flag, or an `AbortController` that cancels the previous request.

items.prompt:
A flex child containing a long unbroken string overflows its container instead of shrinking, even though it has `flex: 1`.

What is going on?

choices.text: `flex: 1` only grows an item, it never shrinks it
A flex item's `min-width` defaults to `auto`, so it will not shrink below its content; `min-width: 0` releases it
The container needs `overflow: hidden`
The string needs `white-space: nowrap` removed

items.explanation: `min-width: auto` on flex items is the single most common cause of an unexplained overflow. `overflow: hidden` hides the symptom by clipping; `min-width: 0` lets the item shrink so the text can wrap or ellipsis properly.

choices.text: Red — it comes first
Blue — it comes last and both have the same specificity (0,2,0)
Red — descendant selectors are more specific
Blue — class-on-class beats descendant

items.explanation: Both selectors are two classes, so specificity is a tie at (0,2,0) and source order decides. Specificity counts the selectors, not how the elements nest.

items.prompt:
A page renders a 5,000-row table and typing in the filter box feels frozen for about a second per keystroke.

Which change addresses the actual cost?

choices.text: Wrap each row in `React.memo`
Render only the rows in view — virtualise the list — so the DOM holds tens of nodes rather than thousands
Move the filter into a `useMemo`
Debounce the input by 300 ms

items.explanation: Debouncing makes the freeze less frequent and just as long; memo and useMemo save re-computation while still asking the browser to lay out 5,000 rows. The cost is the DOM size, so the fix is to stop creating it.

items.prompt: A `<div>` with an `onClick` opens a dialog. It works with a mouse. What is missing for a keyboard user?

choices.text: An `aria-label`
It is not focusable and does not respond to Enter or Space — a `<button>` gives all of that for free
A `cursor: pointer` style
Nothing; click handlers fire on keyboard activation too

items.explanation: A div is not in the tab order and has no activation behaviour. You can bolt on `tabindex`, `role="button"` and key handlers, or use the element that already has them.

items.prompt: A `fetch` to another origin fails in the browser with a CORS error, but the same URL works in Postman. What does that tell you?

choices.text: The API is down for browsers only
The server does not send the CORS headers the browser requires; the restriction is enforced by the browser, not by the server
The request needs an API key that Postman is adding automatically
It can be fixed from the frontend by setting `mode: 'no-cors'`

items.explanation: Postman is not a browser and does not enforce the same-origin policy, so it never checks. The response has to carry the right `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers, which is a server change. `no-cors` does not fix it — it gives you an opaque response you cannot read.

items.prompt:
Users report that a page 'sometimes loads blank' but you cannot reproduce it on your machine.

Describe how you would investigate — what you would look at, and what you would add to the app so that next time you have evidence.

rubric.criterion: Uses real evidence from the failing environment: console/network from the user, error-tracking service, or server logs — rather than only trying to reproduce
Names plausible causes tied to environment differences: a failed request, a JS error in an older browser, a cached stale bundle, a slow network
Proposes adding error reporting or an error boundary so a crash shows something instead of a blank page
Mentions checking on a real device or throttled network rather than only a fast desktop

items.explanation: A blank page almost always means an uncaught error during render. The answer worth full marks stops trying to reproduce and starts collecting: without reporting from the environment where it breaks, you are guessing.

items.prompt:
A team is deciding whether to put the currently-signed-in user, the contents of a form, and a list of products fetched from an API into one global store.

Say which of the three belong in global state and which do not, and explain the rule you are applying.

rubric.criterion: Distinguishes server state (the product list) from client state, and notes it has different needs — caching, refetching, staleness
Keeps form state local, on the grounds that nothing outside the form needs it while it is being edited
Puts the signed-in user in global state, because many unrelated parts of the tree read it
States a general rule — lift state only as far as the components that actually read it

items.explanation: The useful rule is that state belongs at the lowest level where everything that reads it can see it. The sharper distinction is server state versus client state: a fetched product list is a cache of someone else's data, and treating it as ordinary state is what leads to hand-written refetch and invalidation logic.

items.prompt: This component adds a resize listener and never removes it, so a page that mounts it repeatedly accumulates listeners. Fix it, and add a one-line comment naming what the returned function does.

rubric.criterion: Returns a cleanup function from useEffect that removes the listener
The handler is a named/stable reference, so add and remove refer to the same function
Adds a dependency array — `[]` — so the effect does not re-subscribe on every render
The comment correctly describes the returned function as cleanup that runs on unmount (and before a re-run)

items.explanation: Two bugs stack here: no cleanup, and no dependency array, so every render adds another listener. `removeEventListener` compares by identity, which is why an inline arrow cannot be removed — the handler has to be hoisted into a variable the cleanup can name.

items.prompt:
Write a `useDebouncedValue<T>(value: T, delayMs: number): T` hook. It returns the latest value, but only after `delayMs` has passed with no further changes.

It must not leak timers when the value changes rapidly or the component unmounts.

rubric.criterion: Holds the debounced value in state and updates it from a useEffect keyed on [value, delayMs]
Clears the pending timer in the effect's cleanup, so a rapid change cancels the previous one
Initialises the state with the incoming value, so the first render returns something sensible rather than undefined
Generic in T and returns T — no `any`

items.explanation: The whole hook is the cleanup. Without `return () => clearTimeout(t)` every keystroke schedules its own update and they all fire, which is throttling with extra steps rather than debouncing. The cleanup runs before each re-run and on unmount, which handles both leaks at once.
